item.title: How to back up photos to a USB drive without uploading them
item.description: Your photos don't need a cloud to be safe. A USB drive plugged into your phone holds the whole backup — no upload, no monthly fee, no account, and nobody else's server ever sees your pictures.

item.title: USB photo backup on Android: back up photos to an external drive without uploading them
item.description: Your phone's camera roll fits on a drive you can hold. A USB photo backup keeps the whole copy in your pocket — no upload, no monthly fee, no account, and nobody else's server ever sees your pictures.

item.title: How to back up DCIM to OTG storage on Android
item.description: DCIM is where your Android phone keeps its camera photos — and OTG is how a USB drive plugs straight into that phone. Put the two together and your whole camera roll copies to a drive you can hold, with no computer and no upload in between.

item.title: How to copy photos to a USB stick on Android
item.description: A USB stick is the simplest photo backup there is: no account, no upload, no monthly fee — just your photos on a drive you can hold. And on Android you don't need a computer in between: the stick plugs straight into the phone.

item.title: How to back up photos offline on Android — no cloud, no account
item.description: Most "backup" apps start by uploading your photos to someone else's server. An offline backup never does: your photos copy from your phone straight to a drive you can hold, with no account, no upload, and nothing to log into.

item.title: How to back up photos to an external drive on Android
item.description: An external drive is the simplest photo backup there is: a drive you can hold, with your photos on it, and no cloud in between. On Android the drive plugs straight into the phone — no computer needed.

item.title: How to free up space by moving photos to a USB drive
item.description: Your phone is full because your photos are. Move them to a USB drive you can hold, check the copy, then delete the originals — and the storage warning goes away without losing a single picture.

item.title: SnapDisk vs VaultDrive: USB photo backup on Android, compared
item.description: Two Android apps that copy your photos to a USB drive — no cloud, no account, no upload. Here is how they actually differ, from the facts we could verify as of November 2026.

item.title: Back up WhatsApp photos to a USB drive on Android (no computer)
item.description: Your WhatsApp photos are files on your phone — in a folder you can point a backup app at. Plug a USB drive into the phone and copy them straight to it, no computer, no upload.

item.title: Transfer photos from Android to a USB drive automatically (no manual copy)
item.description: Moving photos to a USB drive by hand means opening a file manager, picking files one by one, and hoping nothing gets missed. Plug the drive in, tap once, and let the whole library copy itself.

item.title: Back up Samsung Galaxy photos to a USB drive (no computer)
item.description: Galaxy phones are the most common Android phones there are, and Samsung gives you two ways to get photos onto a USB drive — but neither one is a photo backup that runs itself. Here is what Samsung offers, and the one-tap version.

item.title: Back up Google Pixel photos to a USB drive (no computer)
item.description: Pixel phones have no SD-card slot and no Samsung-style file manager — but a USB-C flash drive plugs straight in, and the stock route is Files by Google. Here is the manual way, and the one-tap version.

item.title: Back up OnePlus photos to a USB drive (no computer)
item.description: OnePlus phones hide one extra switch before a USB drive works at all — OxygenOS turns OTG off unless you enable it. Once it's on, a USB-C flash drive plugs straight in, and the stock route is My Files. Here is the manual way, and the one-tap version.

item.title: Back up Xiaomi photos to a USB drive (no computer)
item.description: Xiaomi phones hide one extra switch before a USB drive works at all — on many MIUI and HyperOS phones OTG is off unless you enable it, and it switches itself off after about 10 minutes. Once it's on, a USB-C flash drive plugs straight in, and the stock route is Mi File Manager. Here is the manual way, and the one-tap version.

item.title: Back up Motorola photos to a USB drive (no computer)
item.description: Motorola phones run near-stock Android, so there is no OTG switch to hunt for — a USB-C flash drive plugs straight in, and the stock route is Files by Google. Here is the manual way, and the one-tap version.

item.title: Back up videos from Android to a USB drive (no computer)
item.description: Videos are the files that fill a phone first — and the ones the manual copy handles worst, one long file at a time. Here is the manual way, and the one-tap version.

item.title: Back up Huawei photos to a USB drive (no computer)
item.description: Huawei phones have their own built-in backup app, but it writes an encrypted archive — not plain photos you can open anywhere. A USB-C flash drive plugs straight in, and the stock route is the Files app. Here is the manual way, and the one-tap version.

item.title: Back up Sony Xperia photos to a USB drive (no computer)
item.description: Sony's Xperia phones run near-stock Android with almost no Sony apps on board — Google Photos is the gallery, Files by Google is the file manager — and Sony's own backup tool needs a PC. A USB-C flash drive plugs straight in. Here is the manual way, and the one-tap version.

item.title: Back up LG photos to a USB drive (no computer)
item.description: LG stopped making phones in 2021, so no LG guide or LG tool will ever be written for this — and LG's own backup tools move data phone-to-phone or phone-to-PC, never phone-to-USB as plain photos. A USB-C flash drive plugs straight in. Here is the manual way, and the one-tap version.

item.title: Back up Oppo photos to a USB drive (no computer)

A USB-C flash drive plugs straight in once the switch is on. Here is the manual way, and the one-tap version.

item.title: Back up Realme photos to a USB drive (no computer)

item.title: Back up Vivo photos to a USB drive (no computer)

A USB-C flash drive plugs straight in once the switch is on. Here is the manual way, and the one-tap version.

item.title: Back up Honor photos to a USB drive (no computer)

A USB-C flash drive plugs straight in. Here is the manual way, and the one-tap version.

item.title: Back up Nokia photos to a USB drive (no computer)

item.title: Back up Asus photos to a USB drive (no computer)

item.title: Back up Infinix photos to a USB drive (no computer)

item.title: Back up Tecno photos to a USB drive (no computer)

Here is the manual way, and the one-tap version.

item.title: Back up Nothing Phone photos to a USB drive (no computer)
item.description: Nothing phones (Phone (1), Phone (2), Phone (2a), and the CMF Phone 1) run Nothing OS — a near-stock Android skin — with OTG support on the main Phone models: spec tables list USB Type-C 2.0 with OTG for the Phone (1), Phone (2), Phone (2a), and Phone (2a) Plus, and Nothing's own support site documents OTG as a feature — but the CMF Phone 1 is the exception to check, because spec tables disagree on whether it supports OTG at all. A USB-C flash drive plugs straight into any Nothing phone. Here is the manual way, and the one-tap version.

A USB-C flash drive plugs straight into any POCO phone. Here is the manual way, and the one-tap version.

And iQOO's own backup tools are iQOO Cloud (vivo Cloud) and Google's — Google Photos and Google backup — plus PC tools, which back your photos up to the cloud or to a computer, not to a USB drive as plain files. And HTC has no phone-to-USB backup tool of its own: its own tool is HTC Sync Manager, a desktop app that backs your pictures up to a PC — and it is discontinued, support ended — and the other routes are Google's — Google Photos and Google backup — which back your photos up to the cloud, not to a USB drive as plain files. A USB-C flash drive plugs straight into any current HTC. Here is the manual way, and the one-tap version.

item.title: Back up Blackview photos to a USB drive (no computer)

A USB-C flash drive plugs straight into any current Blackview. Here is the manual way, and the one-tap version.

item.description: Sonim's Android phones (XP8 and XP10) have USB host support on at least the XP8 — the XP8 user guide lists the USB-C port as "High Speed, OTG" — and Sonim has no phone-to-USB backup tool of its own: Sonim SCOUT is a device-management app, not a backup, and the stock photo backup is Google Photos. One honest caveat up front: the XP10 datasheet I found does not list OTG either way, so check Settings > Storage before relying on it, and the XP5s is not an Android phone at all — it runs a proprietary OS, so SnapDisk cannot install on it. Here is the manual way, and the one-tap version.

item.title: Back up Kyocera photos to a USB drive (no computer)
item.description: Kyocera's DuraForce Android phones (Pro 2, Ultra 5G, PRO 3, and DuraSport) have USB host support on at least two of them — the spec tables list USB OTG as Yes for the DuraForce Pro 2, and the DuraSport's spec pages list its port as "USB Type-C, USB On-The-Go" — and Kyocera has no phone-to-USB backup tool of its own: its backup advice is a computer copy or Google Drive and Google Photos in the cloud. One honest caveat up front: the Hammer 6 LTE is a feature phone, not an Android phone at all, so SnapDisk cannot install on it, and the original Hammer Iron runs Android 4.2 and the AXE M LTE runs Android 6.0, below SnapDisk's Android 7.0 minimum. Here is the manual way, and the one-tap version.

item.title: Back up FOSSiBOT photos to a USB drive (no computer)
item.description: FOSSiBOT's rugged F-series Android phones (F101, F101 Pro, F102, F107 Pro, F110 Pro 5G, F112 Pro, and F113) list USB OTG support in their spec tables, and FOSSiBOT has no phone-to-USB backup tool of its own: its backup advice is a computer copy or Google Drive and Google Photos in the cloud. Here is the manual way, and the one-tap version.

item.title: Back up UMIDIGI Bison photos to a USB drive (no computer)

Three honest caveats up front: USB host is confirmed in the 2021 datasheet only for the UL20X, the UL20W and the UL20F — the datasheet lists a USB 2.0 Host (A type) port alongside a USB 2.0 Client (C type) port — while the base UL20's own spec sheet names only a USB-C port via snap-on or cradle and no host port, so plug a drive in and check Settings > Storage on the base UL20 before relying on it; no source found assigns one Android version to one variant — the datasheet gives Android 8.1, 9.0 GMS and 10 GMS for the series, the original UL20 spec sheet says Android 8.1, a retailer lists the UL20 on Android 10, and a university listing puts the UL20X on Android 9.0 GMS — so check Settings > About phone if you are unsure which version your unit runs; and no source found uses the word OTG for the UL20 at all, so this article says host, not OTG, throughout. Here is the manual way, and the one-tap version.

item.title: Back up Handheld photos to a USB drive (no computer)
item.description: The refreshed Nautiz X2, the Nautiz X6, the Nautiz X9, the Nautiz X41 and the Nautiz X81 are Handheld Group's Nautiz line of rugged enterprise Android handhelds (refreshed X2; X6; X9; X41; X81), and Handheld has no phone-to-USB backup tool of its own: no Handheld-specific file advice pointing at a USB drive turned up at all. Four honest caveats up front: OTG or host is confirmed in the datasheets on all five models that can run SnapDisk — the refreshed X2 and the X9 list OTG on micro-USB, the X6 and the X41 list OTG on USB-C, and the X81 has a USB A host port on its bottom panel — but the adapter differs by model: only the X81 takes a standard USB-A drive with no adapter, the X2 and the X9 need a micro-USB OTG adapter, and the X6 and the X41 need a USB-C OTG adapter; three older Nautiz models cannot run SnapDisk at all — the original Nautiz X2 runs Android 6.0, the Nautiz X4 runs Android 4.2 or Windows Embedded Handheld 6.5, and the Nautiz X8 runs Android 4.2.2 or Windows Embedded Handheld 6.5.3 — all below SnapDisk's Android 7.0 minimum, so the computer copy in Method 4 is the route on those; two Android versions differ by source — the X2 is Android 6.0 in its original datasheet and Android 9.0 GMS in its refreshed datasheet, the X6 is Android 8.0 in its datasheet and Android 8.1 in Rugged PC Review's lineup note, and the X9 is Android 7.0 in its datasheet while a later Handheld press release puts the X9 on Android 11 — so check Settings > About phone if you are unsure which version or generation your unit runs; and no source found names the stock file manager on a Nautiz handheld, so Method 2 uses the built-in file manager, whatever it is called on your unit. Here is the manual way, and the one-tap version.

item.title: Back up Winmate photos to a USB drive (no computer)
item.description: The M700DQ8-EX, the M700DQ9, the M700DM9, the M900MGN, the P400M9 and the G900G7 are Winmate's rugged Android tablets and handhelds (M700DQ8-EX; M700DQ9; M700DM9; M900MGN; P400M9; G900G7), and Winmate has no phone-to-USB backup tool of its own: no Winmate-specific file advice pointing at a USB drive turned up at all. Four honest caveats up front: the adapter differs by model — the M900MGN and the G900G7 take a standard USB-A flash drive straight into their USB 3.0 Type-A port with no adapter at all, while the M700DQ8-EX, the M700DQ9, the M700DM9 and the P400M9 have only a USB-C OTG port, so a USB-A drive needs a USB-C OTG adapter (or a USB-C dual drive) — and on the G900G7 neither Winmate nor the reseller listing labels the Type-C port OTG, so use the Type-A port for the drive; two Android versions differ by source — the M700DQ9 is Android 15.0 in its spec table, Android 13 in its page body, and Android 11 in a summary line on the same Winmate page, and the P400M9's screen is 4.0 inches in its spec table and 4.3 inches in its FAQ while its battery is 2,700 mAh in the spec table and "typically around 3000-4000mAh" in the FAQ — so check Settings > About phone if you are unsure which version your unit runs; no source found states a camera spec for the M700DQ9, the M700DM9 or the G900G7, or a microSD capacity for any of the six models — every covered model has a microSD slot, but no source states how large a card it takes — and no source found names the stock file manager on a Winmate device, so Method 2 uses the built-in file manager, whatever it is called on your unit; and three Winmate models turned up but are not covered — the M700DM8 turned up by name only in accessory listings, the G500G7 is a 5.5-inch ARM Android rugged handheld controller, but no source found states its Android version or labels either of its two USB-C ports OTG, and the G900AD runs Windows, so it cannot run SnapDisk at all. Here is the manual way, and the one-tap version.

item.title: Back up Juniper Systems photos to a USB drive (no computer)
item.description: The Mesa 3 (Android), the Archer 4 and the Archer 3 are Juniper Systems' rugged Android handhelds and tablets (Mesa 3; Archer 4; Archer 3), and Juniper has no phone-to-USB backup tool of its own: no Juniper-specific file advice pointing at a USB drive turned up at all. Five honest caveats up front: the adapter differs by model — the Archer 3 takes a standard USB-A flash drive straight into its full-size USB host port with no adapter at all, while the Mesa 3 and the Archer 4 have only a USB-C OTG port, so a USB-A drive needs a USB-C OTG adapter (or a USB-C dual drive); the Mesa 3's Android version differs by source — Android 9.0 at launch in Juniper's 2020 datasheet, Android 11 (GMS) in the current reseller spec — so check Settings > About phone if you are unsure which version your unit runs; the Archer 3 has no Google Play Store at all — it runs Android 7.1 AOSP with no Google Mobile Services, so install SnapDisk there by sideloading the APK, and its 5 MP camera is optional, not standard; the Mesa 3's OTG port does not charge the battery — its spec table says "USB-C, USB 3.1 OTG no battery charging" — so back up with a charged battery, because the drive occupies the only USB-C port; and no source found names the stock file manager on a Juniper device — the Archer 3 owner's manual lists the preloaded apps (Calculator, Calendar, Camera, Gallery, Music, Opera) and no file manager is among them — so Method 2 uses the built-in file manager, whatever it is called on your unit, and on the Archer 3 you may need to install one first. Here is the manual way, and the one-tap version.

item.title: Back up Trimble photos to a USB drive (no computer)
item.description: The TDC600 and the TDC650 are Trimble's rugged Android GNSS handhelds (TDC600; TDC650), and Trimble has no phone-to-USB photo backup tool of its own: its USB transfer docs move survey job files, not photos. Five honest caveats up front: neither datasheet labels the USB-C port OTG — both say only USB 3.0 (Type-C) — so plug in a drive and look for the mount notification, or run a USB OTG Checker app, before buying an adapter; the TDC600's Android version differs by source — Android 8.0 at launch in Trimble's 2019 datasheet, Android 10 in its 2021 FAQ and 2023 datasheet — so check Settings > About phone if you are unsure which version your unit runs; both handhelds are Google Mobile Services certified, so the Play Store is present and no sideload is needed; the TDC650's Android security updates ran until December 2024, per its datasheet footnote; and no source found names the stock file manager on a Trimble handheld — Trimble Mobile Manager is pre-installed on the TDC650, but it manages the device, it is not a file manager — so Method 2 uses the built-in file manager, whatever it is called on your unit. Here is the manual way, and the one-tap version.

item.title: Back up Galaxy XCover photos to a USB drive (no computer)
item.description: The XCover7 Pro, the XCover6 Pro, the XCover7, the XCover5, the XCover Pro, the XCover4s, the XCover4 and the XCover FieldPro are Samsung's rugged Galaxy XCover phones (XCover7 Pro; XCover6 Pro; XCover7; XCover5; XCover Pro; XCover4s; XCover4; FieldPro), and Samsung has no XCover-specific phone-to-USB backup tool of its own: its own USB backup guide is a generic Galaxy Smart Switch guide, not an XCover guide. Five honest caveats up front: OTG is confirmed on only three of the eight — the XCover6 Pro, the XCover5 and the XCover7 Pro — while the XCover7, the XCover Pro, the XCover4s, the XCover4 and the FieldPro have no source that labels their USB port OTG, so plug in a drive and look for the mount notification before buying an adapter; two sources contradict each other on OTG — PhoneBunch says "Not Supported" for the XCover7 Pro, the XCover5 and the XCover6 Pro, while Three lists the XCover6 Pro and the XCover5 as OTG compatible and neoteo, Smartprix, Kimovil and PhoneDB list OTG on the XCover7 Pro — and PhoneBunch's column is not trusted here, because it also denies OTG on the XCover6 Pro, which three other sources confirm; the XCover6 Pro's USB version differs by source — USB Type-C 3.2 in GSMArena and neoteo, USB Type-C 2.0 in a reseller listing — and the XCover Pro's microSD capacity differs by source too, up to 512 GB in one comparison and up to 1 TB in a manual listing, so this article states no capacity for the XCover Pro; the XCover4 is the only covered model with micro-USB instead of USB-C, so it needs a micro-USB OTG adapter, and it launched on Android 7.0, exactly SnapDisk's minimum; and every covered XCover has a removable battery, which is good news for a long backup — the drive occupies the only USB port while it copies, so carry a charged spare instead of counting on charging mid-backup. Here is the manual way, and the one-tap version.

item.title: Back up i.safe MOBILE photos to a USB drive (no computer)
item.description: The IS530.1, the IS530.2, the IS530.RG, the IS530.M1, the IS540.1, the IS540.2 and the IS655 are i.safe MOBILE's intrinsically safe Android smartphones (IS530.1; IS530.2; IS530.RG; IS530.M1; IS540.1; IS540.2; IS655), and i.safe MOBILE has no phone-to-USB backup tool of its own: its manuals point at Google's Android support pages for operating-system questions, not at any i.safe backup app. Five honest caveats up front: no source found labels any i.safe MOBILE USB port OTG — every datasheet and manual says only that the USB interface is for charging and data transfer — so plug in a drive and look for the mount notification, or run a USB OTG Checker app, before buying an adapter; i.safe's own manuals say to use the USB interface only outside explosion-hazardous areas — wired USB connections are prohibited inside them, and only approved accessories may be connected to it — so do the backup outside the hazardous area, with the i.safe PROTECTOR 2.0 cable the device shipped with; the Android version differs by source on two models — the IS540.1 runs Android 12 at launch in one benchmark listing and Android 14 in a reseller listing, and the IS530.2 runs Android 13 in its 2024 datasheet but Android 10, upgradable to 13, in an older reseller sheet — so check Settings > About phone if you are unsure which version your unit runs; the IS655 is the only covered model with micro-USB instead of USB-C, so it needs a micro-USB OTG adapter, and its battery is integrated, not replaceable; and Google Play comes with the EEA versions only — the manuals say the EEA version comes with the Google app and Google Play, and some variants, such as the mining versions, may not have them — so check for the Play Store on your unit, and sideload the APK if it is absent. Here is the manual way, and the one-tap version.

item.title: Back up Ecom Smart-Ex photos to a USB drive (no computer)
item.description: The Smart-Ex 02 DZ1, the Smart-Ex 02 DZ2, the Smart-Ex 02M, the Smart 02, the Smart-Ex 03 DZ1, the Smart-Ex 03 DZ2 and the Smart-Ex 03 CLASSIC MODE are Ecom's (Pepperl+Fuchs) intrinsically safe Android smartphones (Smart-Ex 02 DZ1; Smart-Ex 02 DZ2; Smart-Ex 02M; Smart 02; Smart-Ex 03 DZ1; Smart-Ex 03 DZ2; Smart-Ex 03 CLASSIC MODE), and Ecom has no phone-to-USB backup tool of its own: no source found names one, and the Smart-Ex 02 safety manual lists only the device, its accessories and its safety rules. Five honest caveats up front: the Smart-Ex 02 line has no standard USB port at all — only a 7-pin waterproof magnetic USB 2.0 connector — and no source found says that connector hosts a USB drive, so on the four 02 models the whole method is unconfirmed until a drive mounts through ecom's own cable; no source found labels the Smart-Ex 03's USB Type-C port OTG either — its datasheets say only "Charging via USB Type C" — so on the three 03 models the drive mounting is the test before buying an adapter; the Android version differs by source on three models — the Smart-Ex 03 runs Android 13 in its 2024–2025 datasheets but Android 15 as the latest firmware on ecom's current product pages, the Smart-Ex 02M runs Android 9 as its latest firmware with an upgrade to Android 11 available, and the Smart-Ex 02's processor is the Snapdragon 450 in ecom's datasheet but the Snapdragon 480 5G in a benchmark listing — so check Settings > About phone if you are unsure which version your unit runs; the Smart-Ex 03 takes no microSD card at all — ecom's datasheets carry the note "no SD Card memory extension" — while the Smart-Ex 02 line takes microSD up to 128 GB, so on a 03 the USB drive is the only local copy that leaves the device; and the Smart-Ex 01 runs Android 4.4 at launch (Android 5.1 on its product page), below SnapDisk's Android 7.0 minimum, so it cannot run SnapDisk at all and is not covered here. Here is the manual way, and the one-tap version.

item.title: Back up Bartec photos to a USB drive (no computer)
item.description: The PIXAVI Phone, the PIXAVI Thermal, the PIXAVI Cam, the SP9EX1 Smartphone and the SP9EX1 Smartphone Cam are Bartec's intrinsically safe Android smartphones (PIXAVI Phone; PIXAVI Thermal; PIXAVI Cam; SP9EX1 Smartphone; SP9EX1 Smartphone Cam), and Bartec has no phone-to-USB backup tool of its own: no source found names one, and the PIXAVI user guide lists only the device, its accessories and its safety rules. Five honest caveats up front: the PIXAVI line has no standard USB port at all — only a magnetic USB connector — and no source found says that connector hosts a USB drive, so on the three PIXAVI models the whole method is unconfirmed until a drive mounts through Bartec's own USB Safe Box cable; no source found labels the SP9EX1's USB-C port OTG either — its datasheets list only a "USB-C Port" under External I/O — so on the two SP9EX1 models the drive mounting is the test before buying an adapter; the Android version differs by source on two models — the PIXAVI Phone runs Android 9 in its 2022 datasheet but Android 11 in its 2023 datasheet, and the Impact X runs Android 4.2.2 at launch, Android 5.1.1 after the 2016 update, and Android 7.1.2 in one reseller listing for the updated version — so check Settings > About phone if you are unsure which version your unit runs; the PIXAVI Cam is end-of-life — one reseller marks it "EOL — No longer available for purchase" — and the Agile X and Agile S are Windows tablets, not Android phones, so they cannot run SnapDisk at all and are not covered here; and Bartec's user guide says the USB port may be used for charging only in a non-hazardous area and to use only Bartec approved chargers and cables — so do the backup outside the hazardous area, and your site's own rules govern inside one. Here is the manual way, and the one-tap version.

item.title: Back up iData photos to a USB drive (no computer)
item.description: The iData 95, the K1, the K1S, the K3S, the K8, the K8 Pro, the K8 Pro Cold, the T1, the T1 Pro and the T3 are iData's Android handheld data terminals (iData 95; K1; K1S; K3S; K8; K8 Pro; K8 Pro Cold; T1; T1 Pro; T3), and iData has no phone-to-USB backup tool of its own: no source found names one, and iData's own documentation covers scanning engines, device APIs and device management, not photo backup. Five honest caveats up front: there is no iData 95S — the searches for it return Newland's MT95, a different brand's handheld already covered in its own guide, so the iData 95 line here is the iData 95 itself and the 95W; no source found labels the iData 95's USB port OTG, so on that one model the drive mounting is the test before buying an adapter, while the other nine list "OTG Interface: Support" in their datasheets; the Android version differs by source or by variant on three models — the K1S runs Android 9.0 (GMS) or Android 11.0 (GMS) in iData's own datasheet, the T1 runs Android 9.0 in its Chinese version and Android 10.0 in its GMS version, and the iData 50 runs Android 6.0 in its datasheet but Android 9.0 in one Octopus variant listing — so check Settings > About phone if you are unsure which version your unit runs; no source found states microSD support or a microSD capacity for any covered iData model, or a camera spec for the K1S, K3S, K8, K8 Pro, K8 Pro Cold, T3 or iData 95 — only the K1 (13 MP, optional), the T1 and the T1 Pro (13 MP rear, 5 MP front) carry a camera spec in the sources found; and the iData 50, the iData 55HC and the iData 95W run Android 6.0, below SnapDisk's Android 7.0 minimum, so they cannot run SnapDisk at all and are not covered here. Here is the manual way, and the one-tap version.

item.title: Back up Spectralink photos to a USB drive (no computer)
item.description: The Versity 92, the Versity 95, the Versity 96 and the Versity 97 are Spectralink's enterprise Android smartphones (Versity 92; Versity 95; Versity 96; Versity 97), and Spectralink has no phone-to-USB backup tool of its own: no source found names one, and Spectralink's own software is device management (AMIE) and workplace communication apps (Biz Phone, Push-to-Talk, SAFE), not photo backup. Five honest caveats up front: no source found labels any Versity USB port OTG — the datasheets say only "USB3.1 Type-C Connector" — so on all four series the drive mounting is the test before buying an adapter; the Android version differs by source or by date on the 95 and the 96 — both launched on Android 8.1, later datasheets list Android 10, and both are upgradeable to Android 13, but the upgrade requires a factory default that wipes the device, so back up before upgrading — while the 92 runs Android 10.0 at release with no upgrade to Android 13 stated in any source found, and the 97 runs Android 13; no source found states microSD support or a microSD capacity for any covered Versity model, or a front-camera spec for the 97 — only the 92 (8 MP rear, 2 MP front), the 95 and the 96 (13 MP rear, 8 MP front) and the 97 (16 MP rear with HDR) carry a camera spec in the sources found; the 96 ships Google Mobile Services and the 97 is Google Android Enterprise Recommended, so the Play Store is present there, but no source found states whether the 92 or the 95 ship Google Play, so check for the Play Store on your unit and sideload the APK if it is absent; and Spectralink's DECT handsets and its 84-series Wi-Fi phones are not Android smartphones at all — the DECT 7000 series has no camera and no Android, and the 8440, 8450, 8452 and 8453 have no camera and no memory card — so none of them can run SnapDisk and none is covered here. Here is the manual way, and the one-tap version.
